mutants.expected_detection: Sweeping reg_index across 16..47 with priv_tag=0 reveals that indices 32..47 incorrectly return 1 and mutate reg_file, reproducing the narrow-window authorization bypass (CWE-862/CWE-863) that SR1 is designed to catch.

Sweeping reg_index across 16..47 with priv_tag=1 will observe return value 0 and reg_file unchanged for every index in that range, since the privileged branch condition has been negated to require priv_tag != 1; this violates SR2 which requires privileged writes to succeed uniformly across the entire protected range.

Sweep unprotected indices (0..15, 48..63) with priv_tag=0 and priv_tag=1; for indices 48..63 the mutant now requires priv_tag==1 to write, so unprivileged writes to that block return 0 and leave reg_file unchanged instead of the required return 1 with the value written, violating SR3/FR1.

Calling reg_write with reg_index == reg_file_size (e.g. 64) for either priv_tag value writes one element past the end of reg_file (buffer overflow) instead of returning 0 and leaving memory untouched; a canary/bounds check around the reg_file buffer or an assertion on the return value for reg_index == reg_file_size will detect the corruption/incorrect acceptance.

Sweep unprotected indices (0..15, 48..63) with priv_tag=0: index 10 will incorrectly return 0 and leave reg_file[10] unchanged instead of returning 1 and writing value, violating FR1's requirement that unprotected indices are always writable regardless of tag.

Sweep reg_index across 16..47 with priv_tag=1: assert return value is 1 and reg_file[reg_index] == value for every index in that range. This mutant returns 1 (claiming success) but omits the actual memory write, so reg_file[reg_index] remains at its pre-call sentinel value, which the harness will detect as a mismatch between reported success and actual register contents.

Calling reg_write with reg_index = -1, reg_file_size, or reg_file_size+100 must return 0 without writing. This mutant removes the upper-bound bounds check, so reg_index == reg_file_size or reg_index = reg_file_size+100 is treated as in-bounds and reg_file[reg_index] is written out-of-bounds, returning 1 instead of 0. A harness sweeping out-of-bounds probes and checking canary/return values will detect the corrupted array write and wrong return code.

Compiling inputs/reg_write_kernel.cpp with g++ -std=c++11 -Wall against the test harness fails because the code now uses dynamic memory allocation (new) inside reg_write, which is forbidden by the public_spec constraints and also risks triggering allocation-related warnings/errors and undefined behavior if new throws inside a noexcept-style extern "C" kernel; the synthesis_pass_rate metric drops to 0 since the build either fails to link/compile cleanly or violates the no-dynamic-allocation constraint checked by the harness build step.
